O n 3 July this year, pastor Ezra Jin Mingri was suddenly whisked out of his Chinese jail cell and put on a flight to Los Angeles, where he was reunited with his family after eight years.
His release came as a surprise even to the 56-year-old leader of the prominent underground Zion Church , who had spent almost nine months in a jail cell following a nationwide crackdown on churches Beijing deemed unauthorised . He says Chinese officials told him he was guilty of all charges, but he was allowed to leave.
Pastor Jin was reportedly released after US president Donald Trump said he raised the issue personally with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during their meeting in Beijing in May. Trump had said Xi responded that he would give the request serious consideration.
It was among the rare instances in which China bowed to pressure and released a detained prisoner.
With Xi arriving in the US for talks, Trump is facing renewed calls to press for the release of the other detained pastors and express concern over the alleged crackdown on Christians in China. Jin hopes the issue of religious freedom will be discussed at the meeting between Trump and Xi.
"When I first found out, it was so sudden, so it felt very unreal," he tells The Independent in a interview translated by his daughter, Grace Drexel.
"It was very exciting to be home with my family. It was wonderful," he says, recalling the moment he met Grace's third child and his one-month-old grandchild for the first time.
After enduring immense mental and physical pressure, he walked free on American soil on 4 July as America celebrated its Independence Day. But Pastor Jin says the joy was subdued after he learned that eight other leaders of the church were still behind bars along with other pastors in separate prisons across China.
"Because historically, human rights and religious freedom have not been paid attention to, especially in China," he added.
He adds that since Trump was able to secure his release, "I hope that during president Xi's visit, the other eight pastors will be released”.
Jin was arrested at his home in Beihai in Guangxi province on 10 October 2025 along with dozens of others. He says the conditions at the detention centre were terrible. "It was not something that I've ever experienced before," he adds.
While he didn't experience physical torture, the pastor says he has heard of other Christian leaders from other churches being tortured inside the prison.
Grace tells The Independent that for her father, the prison conditions were extremely tense. "Everything that you do can be used against you. It's a very humiliating state where even if you wanted to use the bathroom, you had to raise your hand," she adds.
She says her father looked noticeably frail and much thinner upon his return to the US. “Even weeks later, he couldn't walk straight. He was kind of wobbling as he was walking. And he just needed new medication,” she says.
“And so we are working on keeping his blood sugar levels and monitoring it so that he gets proper medication,” she adds.
Since his release from prison, Pastor Jin says the campaign against the Christian faith appears to have accelerated. He said raids and arrests have continued across the country, while members of his Church face harassment.
“After my release, they tried to ram the cases through the system and tried to give the other eight cases a quick trial and make them have long sentences,” he said. “Right now they are again pressuring the lawyers. There's a lot of pressure on the lawyers,” he adds.
Other church leaders, including Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife, Pang Yu, are behind bars, he says, with their cases likely to go to trial soon.
President Xi is accused of cracking down on religious freedom through the communist party’s policy of "Sinicisation", a term officials use to describe the adjustment of religion to fit Chinese culture as interpreted by the party.
The government is also accused of cracking down on independent Christian congregations over the past decade, destroying crosses, burning Bibles, shuttering churches, and ordering followers to sign papers renouncing their faith.
Christianity maintains a strong presence in communist-governed China. By official estimates, there are 38 million Protestants and six million Catholics in the country. Chinese law promises freedom of religion but requires religious groups to register with the state and operate under strict political oversight. Those unwilling to comply are often left with no choice but to worship underground.
Many underground churches were targeted during a nationwide crackdown in 2018 and the Zion Church’s main sanctuary was shut down.
Pastor Jin founded the church in 2007 after quitting the official Protestant church. During the 2018 crackdown, the government placed travel restrictions on him so he could not visit his wife and three children, who had resettled in the US.
During the Covid pandemic, Zion Church membership grew after it starting conducting online prayer sessions, attracting believers who were unable to attend worship at state-sanctioned churches which often shut their doors due to public-health restrictions. The church currently estimates 5,000 regular worshippers across nearly 50 cities.
Nearly two months after last year’s crackdown on the Zion Church, Chinese authorities arrested approximately 100 members of another unofficial protestant church, Yayang Church in Wenzhou, Zhejiang province. At least two dozen of them are reportedly still in detention.
But the Church continues to function.
“In China, for many of the Christians in China, not just Zion Church, but generally, many people continue to have faith and live faithfully, according to the Bible, even with the persecution. And it's the same with Zion Church,” he said.
He said that for Christians inside in prison, there was a sense of pride being there. “It's not because of what I did, but because I'm being truly faithful to the Lord,” he said.

Tensions flared on the eve of a critical week ahead for Paramount Skydance’s proposed $111-billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, amid new urgency for talks aimed at settling antitrust litigation brought by California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and 11 other states.
Over the weekend, opposition intensified to a proposed settlement as details trickled out, including a proposal to establish a bipartisan editorial board to monitor cable news channel CNN, one of Warner’s premier properties that Paramount Chief Executive David Ellison would control along with   CBS News.
It was unclear Sunday whether a proposed settlement would require Paramount to sell off assets — something Bonta repeatedly has insisted upon. Critics of the deal urged Bonta and other state attorneys general to resist pressure to reach a settlement that would allow Ellison’s deal to move forward.
“State Attorneys General, please hang tough against the giant proposed Paramount-Warner Brothers merger,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) wrote on social media late Saturday.
“Paramount, run by the Ellisons, should not own both CBS and CNN. California must not cave and take a deal that leaves both under the same owner,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) wrote .
A resolution would allow David Ellison’s $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to finalize
Bonta and Ellison have made progress in the talks in recent days , according to four people familiar with the matter  not authorized to speak publicly.
However, New York’s Letitia James and at least two other  attorneys general who joined Bonta’s lawsuit in July privately have expressed reservations about the proposed compromises, believing they don’t go far enough to mitigate concerns about the power Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield over the film and TV industries should the merger go through, according to the people familiar with the matter.
Neither James nor Connecticut’s William Tong is on board with Bonta’s proposed settlement, three knowledgeable people said. A potential split within Bonta’s coalition could be a setback because Bonta needs the other state attorneys general who joined his legal effort to sign off on any deal.
California’s top prosecutor blasts Paramount-Warner Bros. conduct as ‘amateur hour.’
Reached for comment Sunday, a spokesperson for Bonta reiterated a statement from last week.
“Potential settlement talks are confidential,” the statement said. “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”
Paramount maintains its deal to bring HBO, CNN, CBS, TBS, Comedy Central and two legendary film and television studios together would create a stronger company that could withstand the fierce competition from tech giants such as Apple, Netflix, Google (which owns YouTube) and Amazon. The two studios, on their own, would not be strong enough  to remain viable in the streaming age, the company has said.
On Thursday, Paramount lawyers plan to demand that U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland require the states and the Writers Guild of America to post a $1.88-billion bond that would cover some of Paramount’s delay-related deal costs should the company eventually prevail.
The states and the WGA, which also sued to block the merger, have balked at the request, which was designed by Paramount to create fissures within the coalition of states, which also include Minnesota, Oregon, Colorado, Connecticut, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Los Angeles’ identity and workers’ livelihoods are at stake, say worried residents who fear that Paramount will leave the state.
Ellison wants the merger finalized by Oct. 1, when his company will be obligated to make a higher payout to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders. The company has threatened to move its Hollywood base from its historic Melrose Avenue lot to Tennessee or Texas should the antitrust battle stretch into October.
The prospective loss of an iconic California business — a century-old film studio that helped establish Hollywood — has rattled state and local politicians, who are fearful of losing more jobs at a time when Los Angeles film production levels already are at alarming lows.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor, have  publicly called on Bonta to settle the suit rather than prepare for a trial next spring. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, Bass’ opponent in the L.A. mayor race, has been one of few California politicians in support of Bonta’s fight.
Paramount’s board has approved David Ellison’s contingency plan to move headquarters from Hollywood as early as this fall, according to people familiar with the situation.
In an opinion essay Sunday, a trio of 1st Amendment and antitrust experts dismissed Paramount’s threat to leave Los Angeles as a ploy that doesn’t make business sense.
“Ellison’s threat is empty, and the AG should call that out — not give into it,” the experts — Fiona Scott Morton, Gene Kimmelman and Norm Eisen — wrote in the Contrarian .
Both Morton, an economics professor at the Yale School of Management, and Kimmelman formerly served in the U.S. Justice Department during Democratic administrations. Eisen, founder of the group Democracy Defenders Action, is helping lead the Block the Merger campaign.
“Paramount [would be] sinking the cost of moving before it knows what businesses it owns and how best to combine and organize them — which makes expensive strategic mistakes inevitable,” the trio wrote. “A company that raises its own costs while leaving behind the most valuable labor in the industry does not threaten California; it threatens itself.”
The group noted Paramount, in its regulatory filings, still lists its Times Square offices in New York as its corporate headquarters — not its Melrose Avenue campus in Hollywood.
“There is also the possibility that Ellison is planning to move Paramount to Tennessee regardless of how the lawsuit resolves,” the group wrote.
Bonta and Paramount have discussed including in any settlement a condition that Paramount would keep its operations in California for a set period, according to people familiar with the proposal but not authorized to comment.
Merger opponents planned a Sunday evening rally outside Bonta’s offices in Oakland to encourage him to stand tough. The group plans subsequent demonstrations this week outside James’ office in New York City and the Paramount lot in Hollywood.
The jockeying comes as President Trump, who favors the Ellison takeover of CNN and Warner Bros.,  has barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of reporting he dislikes.
“Trump just locked CNN out of the White House. Now his billionaire allies want to own it,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) added in a Sunday post . “State attorneys general: Don’t settle. Hold the line. Block this merger.”

FDD’s Behnam Ben Taleblu says Iran’s deeply buried nuclear-linked site poses a growing military challenge as Tehran hardens entrances and rebuilds sensitive facilities.
New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.
The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.
The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.
EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE
An overview of Iran’s Natanz nuclear complex and nearby Pickaxe Mountain, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies.)
The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain .
"We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe," Trump told reporters last week. "I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard."
Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 "Fox & Friends" interview highlighted by the White House , Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew "exactly what’s going on," adding that Washington could "take out Pickaxe" if diplomacy failed.
Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.
TRUMP SAYS US HAS 'MASSIVE' MUNITIONS STOCKPILE, VOWS 'TREASONOUS' LEAKERS BEING HUNTED DOWN
A closer view of tunnel entrances at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, seen in satellite imagery from Aug. 21, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Technologies)
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.
"The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow," Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.
"Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out," he said.
"While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb," Ben Taleblu added. "And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances."
NUCLEAR EXPERTS URGE TRUMP NOT TO LET IRAN STEER TALKS AWAY FROM REGIME'S ATOMIC THREAT
A satellite view shows an overview of the Natanz nuclear facility and Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz, Iran, June 30, 2026 (Vantor/Handout via Reuters)
The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility .
In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was "rapidly moving forward" with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.
The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.
The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations .
CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN
Satellite imagery shows the underlying structure of the rebuilt Taleghan 2 facility at Iran’s Parchin military complex encased within a concrete "sarcophagus," prior to being covered with soil in Feb. 13, 2026. (Vantor Technologies with annotations by ISIS)
Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-authored Security Council resolution that would have extended for another year, until September 2027, the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. The measure received 11 votes in favor, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.
The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the "snapback" mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.
A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored .
"The snapback sanctions… occurred, the United States and this U.N. Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur," Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. "Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions."
Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.
"The president has been clear, and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution, that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon," Waltz said.

Thursday also brought fresh U.N. scrutiny of both Washington and Tehran. An independent U.N. fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe two U.S. strikes on civilian sites in Iran in February constituted war crimes, while separately concluding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. The mission is investigative rather than judicial, and its findings do not themselves constitute criminal judgments.

We're still early in the season, and there has been a surprising lack of upsets so far, and I don't just mean the big ones that nobody saw coming. I mean, in general.
On the season, underdogs are 25-132 in games between FBS opponents. That's a win percentage of only .159, which trails way behind recent seasons. As you can see in the table below, last year underdogs won at a .265 clip.
While that table only goes back to 2021, I have data dating back to the 2014 season, the beginning of the College Football Playoff era. From 2014 through 2025, underdogs had a win percentage of .261 overall. Only once did they finish any season with a win percentage worse than .249. It was the 2015 season when the dogs went 165-600 for a win percentage of .216.
And these results don't seem to be due to much larger spreads earlier in the season, given all the nonconference games. If we limit the data to games that featured a spread of 7.5 points or less, underdogs are 20-39 for a win percentage of .339. From 2014 to 2025, the win percentage in such games was .393. The only season that finished with a worse percentage was, you guessed it, the 2015 season at .327.
So what's going on? I wish I knew. It's possible that we're still early in the season, and the small sample size is skewing the results. Maybe we're due for a generational run of underdogs winning outright from here on out. Or maybe there's something to be said about the top of the sport pulling away from the bottom, even if things have flattened a bit at the top. Or maybe, like 2015, this will prove to be an outlier of a season.
I don't know, but considering I include an "Upset of the Week" pick in this column, and I'm coming off a 1-5 week, I'd really appreciate it if some of these underdogs would start pulling their weight and help me dig out of the hole I've dug myself.
Another week, another big game for Ole Miss , which has knocked off two ranked teams in Louisville and LSU already. Obviously, last week's win over LSU meant a bit more to the Rebels than a typical top-10 win, and that's what leads me to my biggest concern heading into another difficult game.
You know this team put a lot of time and energy -- both physical and emotional -- into the LSU game last week. How do they avoid a letdown? Because if you overlook this Florida team, you're going to find yourself 3-1 real quick. So that fear will likely lead plenty of you to lay the points with Florida, even if Jon Sumrall doesn't understand how his team is favored. I'm opting to avoid the spread, though. No, the one thing I find to be clear about this game is that it's likely to be high-scoring.
We've seen Ole Miss' defense allow 62 points in those wins against Louisville and LSU. Every offseason, there's talk that a Lincoln Riley team may have finally fixed its defense, but then the year begins, and it's pretty clear they haven't. Now, Oregon is coming to town, and it's not just a normal Oregon. It's a pissed-off Oregon. Iowa has been the underdog in 10 conference road games against ranked opponents since the 2014 season. It's 1-9 in those games, but what's more important to our interests is that Iowa has averaged only 12.5 points in those 10 games. articles.title_orig: Needy couples got cash and a spending plan. Results were good — and bad
articles.title_zh: Needy couples got cash and a spending plan. Results were good — and bad
articles.content_orig:
Cash transfers, aimed at lifting families out of poverty, are delivered by mobile pone. Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/via Getty Images hide caption
Since the early 2000s, countries have tried to lift people out of poverty with a simple program — giving them cash.
The idea is that a lump sum will help the poorest of the poor buy food, pay for school fees or build a business — like raising livestock — to make more money.
Study after study has shown these cash transfers are a reliable way to help families in extreme poverty build a source of income and support their own basic needs.
The West African nation of Liberia is one of the countries that has seen success with cash transfers. The average amount that the government gives to a needy household per year is $250, which goes a long way there. The money goes to one member of the household to manage for the whole family.
"One of our key design components is that we target the female in the house," says Aurelius Butler, Liberia's national coordinator for social protection.
Liberia, which is among the 10 poorest countries in the world, has a high rate of gender inequality . Women face harassment and discrimination and lack opportunities in the workplace. In many families, the male head of household typically controls the funds, says Butler, and may not give their partners the money to cover basic needs for themselves and their family — like soap or food. By targeting women in the cash aid program, Butler says the aim is to give them some economic control.
Some men were not happy with that setup.
"A lot of the men reported that they felt like they were being excluded," Butler says.
So Liberia came up with a new approach.
With funding from the World Bank, the Liberian government and the nonprofit organization GiveDirectly designed a new cash transfer experiment: give both partners equal money and an equal say in how to spend it.
There were two goals, according to Sarika Gupta a senior economist at the World Bank and one of the lead researchers on a study about this project: help families generate more income and reduce household tension in a country where nearly 35% of women say they face intimate partner violence — higher than the world average of 27%. The results from the study were released in July.
In 2022, more than 2,300 households in the Maryland and Bomi counties of Liberia received $750 in four installments — more than double the amount typically given to a household in cash aid programs since both partners got an equal payout.
To encourage partners to share in decision making, researchers added a joint financial planning element for half of those families.
"The way joint financial planning works is, we sit down with the couple for about 45 minutes and ask them to detail their plan," Butler says. "Is it to fix something within the house? Is it to maybe just buy food, or is it to invest in education, planting or build a business?"
Since the literacy rate in rural areas is low, the researchers also created posters for each family to document their plans.
"It just had a picture of a family happy together, and then it had empty boxes for them to list their four top spending priorities for the cash transfer that was coming," says Gupta. The couples were also given a stack of stickers to indicate what they wanted if they weren't able to write things down: a stack of books meant education, a stethoscope and syringe meant healthcare.
"And the poster stays with the couple, and they can put it on their wall so they can see it. It's like a constant reminder of what they've kind of committed to," Gupta says.
Gupta and other researchers followed the households for a year after they received the cash. The results showed that planning works.
"Households that received the planning actually were even better off economically than households who received only the cash transfer," Gupta says.
One of the participants is Christian — who only provided her first name for the program. She works on a farm, and her husband gathers latex from trees for rubber making. In the joint planning session they agreed on spending priorities: education, food and home repairs. Christian used her cash to pay school fees for their five kids, buy rice and pay off debt. Her husband bought solar light bulbs and cement to patch their leaky roof.
There was another component to the study. Researchers looked at any past history of partner violence in participating couples, interviewing them before giving the cash and then checking in a year later to see if there had been any issues after the cash was received.
Researchers were surprised by what they found. For most couples, there were no reported incidents. But that was not the case for couples determined to be at high risk for violence based on previous incidents. Even though there was an increase in income from the cash transfer, there was also "an increase in intimate partner violence" — but only among those who'd received the planning session, says Gupta.
"It is quite clear that it's something in the shift about couples deciding together [that led to the increase in violence]," says Amber Peterman , an impact evaluation specialist at UNICEF who was not involved in the research.
The hypothesis that Peterman and Gupta share is that conflict may have occurred if one partner deviated from a plan they both openly committed to.
"Anytime one partner or the other maybe deviates from that plan, the other person kind of can call them out," says Gupta. "And so that there could be that kind of downside to planning" — especially in houses prone to conflict.
The planning also may have shifted the power dynamic from men to women, possibly spurring partner violence, Gupta says. The study notes: "This could either happen directly, if planning gave women more agency in how funds were spent, or indirectly, if planning triggered economic changes that gave women more power."
That's valuable information, says Peterman.
"We know that this add-on [of planning] actually did a lot of good at the household [financial] level, and so I think the question is, how could it be tweaked?" he says.
The researchers are hoping to do it again — provided they can get the funding — and with changes that could help ward off conflict.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu expected to attack Mamdani in UN general assembly speech – latest updates
articles.content_orig:
US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran , which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.
The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.
The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979.
Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons.
No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower.
The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran.
Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes.
“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”
US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared.
He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said.
There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.
Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration.
This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”.
He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex.
With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI.
Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”.
Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

articles.title_orig: Trump invites Putin to Miami for first visit to lower 48 since Obama era
articles.title_zh: Trump invites Putin to Miami for first visit to lower 48 since Obama era
articles.content_orig:
Russia has welcomed the U.S. government's invitation for President Vladimir Putin to attend a G20 summit in Florida later this year, saying it "truly" appreciates the offer, but has not yet decided whether to accept it.
The invite stoked outcry in Europe, where governments have been rearming since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he feared Russia would view it as "encouragement to ​continue ‌its aggressive policies," while the European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said it was "really very, very hard to understand this treatment" of Putin.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said the White House had invited Putin to a G20 meeting in Miami in December, where he could potentially hold talks with U.S. President Donald Trump .
"We think it is an opportunity for him to engage, not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that is an invitation he'll accept," Rubio told reporters. "If there is another opportunity for them to meet and there is a purpose behind the meeting, that would be good," he added.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday that Moscow "truly" appreciates the "kind" invitation.
"We value it. It will be worked on and then agreed upon, and a corresponding decision will be made," Peskov told reporters, according to Russia's state-run news agency RIA Novosti .
Ukraine, which has stepped up attacks on Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs in recent months, has warned it will make the coming winter painful for Russia if a truce cannot be agreed over the coming weeks, while acknowledging it also fears another difficult winter period.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Putin "patient zero" and "the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further."
Diplomatic talks to find a peaceful solution to the war have stalled in recent months as the U.S. has shifted focus to its war against Iran, although negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff traveled to Ukraine for the first time for talks with Zelenskyy earlier this month.
In an interview with Sky News , the EU's Kallas said the U.S. invitation to Putin needed to be discussed with political leaders across the 27-nation bloc.
"But it's clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalize people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians, to ignore the international humanitarian law, to cause as much damage and suffering to people that they can," Kallas said.
"By normalising this, believe me, we will have more of it around the world," she added.

articles.content_orig:
George Russell was fastest in a first Azerbaijan Grand Prix practice session in which Mercedes Formula 1 team-mate Kimi Antonelli stopped on track and both McLaren drivers spent an extended spell in the garage. In what was a disrupted first hour of running on the Baku street circuit, Russell set the fastest time - a 1m45.387s - midway through the session, with the aid of a tow from the Aston Martin of Fernando Alonso along the final straight. That put Russell exactly four tenths up on Max Verstappen, who set his fastest time of the session on his third timed attempt on the single set of soft tyres he and Red Bull used, with Charles Leclerc a mere 0.004s further back - the Ferrari having been marginally up on Russell's Mercedes at the end of the second sector. Lewis Hamilton was fourth in the second Ferrari, with Antonelli's initial hard-tyre time good enough for fifth despite stopping inside the first half of the session. Antonelli had been fastest at that point and was preparing for his first run on the soft tyre when he came to a stop in the runoff area past the Turn 7 right-hander, citing a loss of hydraulic pressure. Oscar Piastri moved up to sixth right at the end of FP1, with he and team-mate Lando Norris both forced to spend time in the McLaren garage while the team checked its upgraded MCL40s. Both cars were eventually sent back out, with a close-up of Norris's McLaren showing a makeshift hold on its bargeboard arrangement. Norris completed 14 laps, setting the 14th-fastest time. Racing Bulls had both cars in the top 10. Liam Lawson, on his return to that cockpit after his three-race stand-in spell at Red Bull, was seventh ahead of Arvid Lindblad - who caused a yellow flag late in the session when he stopped at Turn 7 and had to reverse out. Esteban Ocon - who as reported by The Race is set to lose his drive at the end of the season - was ninth for Haas and briefly stopped in the pit exit in the final two minutes of the session.
Gabriel Bortoleto completed the top 10 ahead of Audi team-mate Nico Hulkenberg. He also stopped in the final minutes and had to have his R26 wheeled behind the barriers. Williams duo Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon were 12th and 13th in the upgraded FW48 . Isack Hadjar's return to the Red Bull cockpit following his recovery from a wrist injury was a truncated one. He'd completed just eight laps when he complained of "something really wrong with the engine", after which Red Bull asked him to use second gear only and return to the pits - from which he did not emerge. Hadjar therefore was consigned to 20th, sandwiched between the two Aston Martins of Alonso and Lance Stroll, both of whom have taken fresh power unit components this weekend.

articles.title_zh: Melania Trump’s home-country leader rips UN ‘double standards’ as Trump promise is revealed
articles.content_orig:
PM Janez Janša says the UN's focus on Gaza has overshadowed other global crises, criticizes Europe's approach to Iran and discusses Slovenia's special relationship with the US through First Lady Melania Trump.
UNITED NATIONS - Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša accused the United Nations of applying double standards to global conflicts, arguing that the international community's focus on Gaza has overshadowed Russia's war in Ukraine and other humanitarian crises, while revealing that President Donald Trump has promised to visit Slovenia, the homeland of first lady Melania Trump .
Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Janša said the international body must give greater attention to conflicts beyond the Middle East rather than concentrating its diplomatic efforts on a single crisis.
"We have to get rid of double standards," Janša said, calling for the U.N. to apply its available diplomatic and security tools equally instead of putting its attention, money and energy into one conflict while neglecting others.
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
Right-wing Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) leader Janez Janša addresses the media after his investiture vote as Slovenia's Prime Minister at the National Assembly in Ljubljana on May 22, 2026. (Jure Makovec / AFP via Getty Images)
The Slovenian leader said he was struck by how extensively Gaza dominated speeches during the opening of the General Assembly , while Ukraine, a war much closer to his country's borders, received comparatively less attention.
For Slovenia and other European countries, he said, Russia's invasion represents an immediate security threat, with no clear indication that Moscow is prepared to negotiate an end to the fighting.
Janša argued that the U.N. was established to prevent such conflicts and should not allow its attention to be consumed by one region.
He also pointed to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria and other humanitarian crises, arguing that the international body must recognize that different countries face different security and humanitarian challenges.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
An office building burns following a Russian drone attack in central Odesa, Ukraine, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Michael Shtekel/AP)
Janša said he intends to raise the issue during his own address to the General Assembly, scheduled for Thursday.
His criticism comes as Slovenia undergoes a significant shift in its foreign policy, particularly toward Israel.
Under the previous government of Prime Minister Robert Golob, Slovenia recognized Palestinian statehood in June 2024 and imposed an arms embargo on Israel in July 2025. The government defended those measures as necessary to protect Palestinian civilians and uphold international law.
Since returning to power, Janša has sought to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Israel, marking a shift from the previous government's more critical approach toward the Jewish state.
Earlier this month, Israel opened its first resident embassy in Slovenia, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar visited the country for talks aimed at expanding political and economic cooperation. The two governments also signed a cooperation program covering education, science, culture, youth and sports through 2030.
Janša described his government's approach as a return to the traditionally good relations between the two countries rather than a dramatic diplomatic realignment.

articles.title_zh: 5 reasons I'm ready to ditch my Pixel 11 Pro for the Motorola Signature 27
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
I’ve been absolutely smitten with the Pixel 11 Pro . Google’s 2026 flagship has been my daily driver for over a month now, and pretty much everything is clicking for me — be it the cameras, design, software, and even performance.
I could see myself using the Pixel 11 Pro for a while to come, but suddenly, I’m questioning if that’ll actually happen. And it’s all Motorola’s fault.
Motorola officially announced the Signature 27 this week, and it’s one of the most impressive Android flagships we’ve seen all year. Motorola seems to be checking every box, and even though I love the Pixel 11 Pro, the Signature 27 is calling my name for a few reasons.
I know a lot of folks don’t care about what their phone looks like, especially if you put it in a case. However, as someone who does appreciate good smartphone design, I’m completely taken aback by the Signature 27 — in a good way.
Finding new ways to stand out in the modern smartphone market is no easy task, but Motorola has managed to do precisely that. The Signature 27’s rear camera housing is unlike anything I’ve seen before. It’s a bit odd and may take some getting used to, but I really appreciate the creativity. I also love the gradual slope up to the camera housing and the unique textures on the two available colors.
I think Google did a fantastic job with the Pixel 11 Pro’s hardware, but what Motorola is doing with the Signature 27 really catches my eye. It would have been very easy to pump out a generic iPhone or Samsung Galaxy copycat, but Motorola did the complete opposite, and I’m here for it.
As much as I appreciate the funky layout of the Signature 27’s cameras, I’m even more excited about what these sensors should be capable of. Motorola has confirmed that the Signature 27 features a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 sensor for the primary camera, along with a 200MP (!!!) periscope telephoto camera. The other two sensors are likely another telephoto camera and an ultrawide camera, both of which should be 50MP sensors.
Getting preemptively excited about the cameras on a Motorola phone may sound crazy, and I understand why; this isn’t a company with a long track record of good camera performance. However, after using the Razr Fold earlier this year, I think the days of bad Moto cameras are finally behind us.
The camera system on the Razr Fold is one of the best I’ve used all year — not just on folding phones, but on all Android phones, regardless of form factor. The sensors are all technically excellent, but what really impressed me was Motorola’s image processing and color science. I didn’t expect to be so blown away by the Razr Fold’s cameras, but that’s what happened. If the Signature 27 takes that foundation and makes it better — which it appears to be doing — we’re in for something special.
Hiding inside the Signature 27’s design is something else I’m really interested in: Qualcomm’s just-announced Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset . Is the name terrible? Yes. But bad branding doesn’t detract from what should be one of the most powerful mobile chips for the remainder of 2026 and for most of 2027.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 is already a monster chip, and the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 has some notable improvements — including a CPU that’s 37% more efficient and 13% faster, plus a GPU that’s 40% more efficient and 44% faster. Considering the excellent efficiency and performance we’ve already seen from Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5-powered phones, the mind wanders at the thought of what a phone like the Motorola Signature 27 with an 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 will be capable of.
For a Pixel 11 Pro user like myself, this is really hard to ignore. I think the Tensor G6 in the Pixel 11 Pro is a very good chip and excellent for almost everyone, but it also doesn’t come close to matching Qualcomm’s silicon — and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is only going to widen that gulf even more.
Will I ever fully utilize the performance of Qualcomm’s newest chip? Almost certainly not. But having that extra horsepower for futureproofing is tempting, and the efficiency gains are even more so.
Of course, an efficient chipset only really matters if it’s paired with a good battery, and this is an area where Motorola has excelled for years. The company regularly outfits its phones with very generous battery capacities, and while the Signature 27’s battery specs have yet to be confirmed, I’d expect it to continue that tradition.
Once again, the Razr Fold is a good reminder of this. That phone has a 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, and in my testing, I regularly got through two days of use on a single charge. Keep in mind that’s on a foldable phone with a much more power-hungry 8.1-inch inner display, plus an older Snapdragon 8 Elite chip.
If Motorola crams a similarly sized battery into the Signature 27 and pairs it with its new Snapdragon chip, we could be looking at a three-day smartphone. And if the Razr Fold and other past Moto phones are anything to go by, that big battery should also be accompanied by very fast wired charging — at least 60W, possibly 90W or more.
By comparison, my Pixel 11 Pro reliably gets me through one full day of use, and its 30W wired charging is about as mediocre as you’d expect. These aren’t dealbreakers for me, but if the Signature 27 can combine everything I already mentioned above with multi-day battery life and rapid charging, sticking it out with the Pixel is going to become mighty tricky.
Finally, there’s the last puzzle piece that ties this all together: availability. The original Motorola Signature , launched at the start of this year, also checked many of the same boxes, but it was never released in the United States. But with the Signature 27, Motorola has confirmed that its new phone will see a proper US release.
We still don’t know how much the Signature 27 will cost, and in a world where RAM and storage prices are off the charts, Motorola may have a difficult time keeping the Signature 27 competitive with its Google and Samsung competition. But even so, just the fact that the Signature will be available for regular purchase in the US is a huge deal.
The US flagship Android market desperately needs more competition , and from everything we’ve seen so far about the Signature 27, it should deliver precisely that. And, selfishly, a US release means replacing my Pixel 11 Pro with the Signature 27 will be a lot easier than if I had to import it.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.content_orig:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu takes to his feet at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York later on Thursday, he does so at a critical point in both his political career and in his country’s long and fractious relationship with the international body.
Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide at the UN, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Those criticisms continue to shape the country’s fractious relationship with the body.
For Netanyahu, appearing in front of the UNGA for the 15th time, the stakes have rarely been higher. Addressing a domestic Israeli audience that polls show to be losing faith in him and his Likud party in the run-up to crucial elections later this year, Netanyahu has already pitched himself as Israel’s primary voice on the international stage.
Nevertheless, analysts say Netanyahu’s address could prove a pivotal moment domestically, amplified by international criticism of Israel and expected to dominate headlines and be carried live across the country’s television networks.
“This is a regular fixture for him,” former Israeli consul general in New York and ex-government adviser, Alon Pinkas, told Al Jazeera. “It’s his way of being seen in Israel as standing up against the world and of telling members that he will never give up or surrender. He’s also turned the event into some kind of national holiday in Israel, with everyone sitting down to watch the address on television. He’s brainwashed people in Israel into believing his speech is somehow an announcement of policy, stated in defiance of the [rest of the world] who don’t believe a word he says.”
Israeli leaders have long framed their stance towards the UN as one of defiance in the face of hostility. The UN has long been a platform for critics of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land and repeated attacks on its neighbours. It has included attempts to censure Israel over what UN investigators have described as apartheid in the West Bank, as well as accusations of genocide and pogroms across the occupied Palestinian territory since October 2023.
There have been numerous UNGA resolutions criticising Israel’s conduct – nearly all dismissed by Israeli lawmakers as evidence of institutional bias – culminating in Israel declaring UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres persona non grata and severely restricting the operations of the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
“Generally speaking, many Israelis tend to see the UN as anti-Israeli,” Nimrod Goren, the president of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, Mitvim, said.
Against that background, criticism from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – already cast as anti-Israel in the Israeli press – has drawn greater public attention to the event. Underscoring the sense of hostility towards Israel are stories within the country’s media suggesting that Netanyahu’s visit to New York has been curtailed due to unspecified security concerns, with the Israeli premier expected to fly out of New York on the same day as his arrival.
In response, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, who has repeatedly accused the organisation of waging “diplomatic terrorism” against the state, called for Mamdani’s arrest for what he said was the mayor’s incitement against New York’s Jewish community before Netanyahu’s visit.
“Netanyahu is going into his UNGA speech with not one but both eyes focused firmly on the upcoming Israeli election,” Goren said. “The speech is usually treated in Israel as a major event, receiving broad coverage and dominating the news cycle. Netanyahu will likely try to leverage this to bolster his image as a close ally of the US and to talk up the threat posed by Iran.”
Some have interpreted US President Donald Trump’s apparent lack of availability to meet Netanyahu during this trip as a sign of waning support. But US backing for Israel at the UN has remained steadfast since the October 7 attack and has contributed to growing frustration within the UN over what they see as Israel’s ability to resist international censure.
Alongside the creation of the Board of Peace, which shifted significant responsibility for Gaza’s future from the UN to the Trump-founded organisation, Washington has repeatedly used its veto at the UN Security Council (UNSC) to shield Israel from resolutions it opposes. The US has vetoed at least six UNSC resolutions on Gaza since October 2023, most of them demanding an immediate ceasefire.
“There seems to be genuine frustration within the UN General Assembly over the body’s failure to play a significant political role in Gaza and the West Bank, but also in its failure to protect its own staff and agencies,” Chatham House Associate Fellow Zizette Darkazally, who previously worked with the UN, said.
“However, it’s worth remembering the context the UN operates within in the occupied territories and the important humanitarian role it plays. The UN continues to get aid and medical support into Gaza and the West Bank, which are both areas where Israel has absolute control over access,” she said. “It’s also worth remembering that the UN is only as strong as the commitment of its member states.
“That, combined with a system of veto that’s more than 80 years old, has left the organisation weaker now than it had ever been,” she said of the confrontations between the UN and Israel. “And we’re seeing the effects of that, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen, Sudan and Iran, where the UN is playing next to no political role.”

They're the first to navigate Survivor 's "Open Era," where the rules of the past are back in play. As host Jeff Probst explained during the Season 50 finale, "Anything that's ever happened on Survivor can happen again — at any time, in any order, without warning."
The Open Era introduces a coin flip that could add another $1 million to the winner's prize. If the flip is lost, that additional money rolls over to the following season.

As fuel prices at the pump reach record highs since the outbreak of the war in Iran, Washington is warming to the idea of a temporary diesel export ban as a way to lower costs.
“I’ve said let's not send out the diesel—we make a lot of diesel,” President Donald Trump said as he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in New York on Tuesday. “That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know, it’s a sort of a flow.”
Trump echoed what a cacophony of Republican lawmakers, many representing farm states, have called for in the past few weeks. Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa posted on social media Saturday : “High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME.” Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, meanwhile, said Tuesday that the cost of diesel “is just too damn high” and an export moratorium should be in place until the conflict in Iran ends.
Diesel recorded its highest average price on Tuesday amid the energy dearth caused by the war, averaging about $6.53 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association . It is at least 90¢ higher than last month’s average, and a huge leap from the $3.75 mean just before the war .
Ballooning prices threaten to impact the global economy as diesel powers most heavy-duty farming and industrial machinery as well as transport like trucks and trains. Higher diesel costs also add to the cost of moving goods and could worsen inflation, which the Federal Reserve has tried to tamp down .
Trump referred to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said that the Administration is examining whether a diesel export ban is “feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.”
It’s unclear if, or when, the Administration will decide on a moratorium on diesel exports. Trump’s own Energy Secretary Chris Wright showed more skepticism: speaking to CBS News earlier this month, Wright said the U.S. is considering “all options of how you can move prices that are favorable for American consumers,” but he also argued that to address a shortage, “you want to keep as much energy flowing as possible.”
Rising costs present a problem for an increasingly unpopular Trump heading into the November midterms, where the Republican Party he leads has to defend its slim majority in Congress. Disgruntled voters, according to some polls , believe the U.S. economy has suffered under Trump’s policies, with many from the GOP also souring on them .
The U.S. is one of the world's largest diesel producers and exporters. Data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration show that American refineries produce about 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel oils—referring to fuels that include diesel and home heating oil—per day. Diesel exports amount to about 1.5 million barrels daily, almost a fifth of the roughly 8 million barrels traded by sea each day.
But since diesel is traded globally, prices in the U.S. are shaped by this balance of supply and demand. The recent price surge has been linked to production and shipping disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Many Republican lawmakers pushing for the diesel export ban argue that it could provide American consumers with some relief. Last week, Rep. Tim Burchett of Tennessee filed bills to address rising diesel costs through export controls and argued that such controls “drive down prices while also helping Americans keep more money in their pockets.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota also indicated that he was “open to exploring” a diesel export ban to lower prices.
Analysts from the Washington think tank Atlantic Council wrote in a Tuesday note that such an export ban “would likely create more problems than it would solve.”
While the ban is expected to “almost certainly” push prices down for consumers in the Gulf Coast and the Midwest, it may pull prices up for those on the West Coast. “If the global price of diesel rises and supplies in the heartland cannot be routed to the coasts quickly enough, then these regions could see higher prices,” the analysts wrote. They also warned of knockon effects including a possible uptick in grocery prices.
Garrett Golding, assistant vice president at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, said in a social media thread on Monday that even with the swift dip in diesel prices, a diesel export ban would tighten the global balance enough to cause price increases that “will boomerang back” onto the East Coast—and to a smaller degree, the West Coast.
Refineries will also have to reduce their run rate—the percentage of a refinery’s maximum capacity used to process crude oil into refined products, Golding added. This would lead to reduced production of gasoline, jet fuel, and other refined products, “which means higher prices.”
The Atlantic Council analysts also warned that an export ban would have follow-on effects outside of the U.S., including pushing international diesel prices up, which could similarly “boomerang” on the country.
The API opposes a ban and argues that doing so risks “making a difficult situation worse.” President and CEO Mike Sommers said in a statement, “We understand the administration is looking at every option to deliver relief, but restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers.”
The diesel export ban has been a point of contention for GOP lawmakers ahead of the November elections. Some from oil-producing states argue against the proposal on the basis that a ban could push prices down for producers under their jurisdiction.
Outgoing Senator John Cornyn of Texas, the largest oil-producing state in the U.S., claimed that the ban is a “gimmick.”
Cornyn’s colleague, Senator Lisa Murkowski of major oil producer Alaska, cast her doubts on the export ban to the Hill : “We’re talking about global supply, so I worry that we do something in the short-term … that doesn’t really move the needle.”
Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota also expressed criticism and said he is instead looking to other options, including restarting idled refineries. “The bigger problem we’ve got right now is, as I understand it, in California, we’ve already lost two more refineries because of California’s strict environmental rules,” Rounds told the Hill . “I would like to get those back up and operational again.”
The reactions exhibit how keen Republicans are to appear that they are providing solutions to the rising costs of living. As Reuters’ energy columnist Ron Bousso put it , fuel costs are increasingly becoming a political liability, and for the wider GOP, “a politically popular ‘quick fix’ may prove difficult to resist.”

Dr. Heidi Overton, a fierce opponent of abortion rights, is set to appear before senators Thursday for her confirmation hearing to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
The hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee comes as the FDA faces pressure from Republicans, including the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., to tighten access to the abortion pill mifepristone.
Cassidy, who is a key vote in Overton’s confirmation, has been pushing the administration to reverse a Biden-era rule that allows mifepristone to be prescribed via telemedicine and sent through the mail.
In a committee report published last month , Cassidy accused the makers of mifepristone of failing to meet their legal responsibilities to ensure compliance with FDA safety regulations, particularly when the pills are sold online through third-party providers. At a hearing in January , Cassidy called on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the previous FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary, to complete a safety review that they both promised during their confirmation hearings. In June, the FDA said it launched a new safety study on mifepristone.
Art Caplan, the head of the medical ethics division at NYU Grossman School of Medicine in New York City, said Overton’s views on abortion appear to align with Cassidy’s.
Overton, a preventive medicine physician, currently serves as a domestic policy official in the White House. Prior to that, she worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute, where she praised the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion, claiming that it is “ dangerous to women .” (Studies have shown that the drug , even when taken at home, is safe and effective.)
If confirmed, Overton would take over an agency that has been without a permanent commissioner since Makary resigned in May, in part over the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vapes for adults.
As commissioner, Overton would serve as a key ally to Kennedy, whose department oversees the FDA. Overton is a proponent of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. She also appeared alongside President Donald Trump in August when he announced an executive order aimed at reducing the number of vaccines routinely recommended for children. Trump nominated her to lead the agency days later.
Senators are likely to grill her about her own views on vaccines, according to Dorit Reiss, a professor of law and vaccine policy expert at the University of California Law San Francisco.
On CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Cassidy — who has also aggressively questioned and pressed several Trump administration nominees on vaccines — said Overton must acknowledge that Trump’s claim that the measles vaccine is lethal is “absurd” when she appears before his committee. Trump made the comment during the August signing of his vaccine executive order.
“I think she made it clear she’s a supporter of Kennedy’s vaccine agenda, at least,” Reiss said. “Dr. Overton seems like another example of an appointee who is, primarily, appointed for political opinions, without an emphasis on qualifications.”
Overton, Reiss said, doesn’t appear to have expertise in clinical trials, managing an agency or any of the products the FDA regulates.
“It’s reasonable for an administration to want someone sympathetic to their views,” Reiss said, “but FDA commissioner is a hard job that requires the ability to manage a large and complex agency that does important work.”
“As an MD/PhD who helped President Trump deliver on Operation Warp Speed during his first term, Dr. Heidi Overton will ensure that policymaking is guided solely by Gold Standard Science at the FDA,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.
Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting FDA commissioner, said food safety will be another major issue waiting for her at the FDA.
The agency has spent much of the summer responding to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks and recalls, including a massive cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce that sickened more than 12,000 people across multiple states.
The outbreak has also raised questions about how quickly the FDA can trace contaminated food back to its source and whether the agency has enough staff to respond to outbreaks after thousands of employees left or were laid off over the past year.
“After the experience of the past 18 months, it’s very important to restore public and industry confidence that decisions being made by FDA, including those by leadership, are science-based, transparent and consistent,” Ostroff said.

articles.title_orig: Questions abound about how US-China 'notification mechanism' on AI will work as summit gets underway
articles.title_zh: Questions abound about how US-China 'notification mechanism' on AI will work as summit gets underway
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Following a weekend of meetings with Chinese officials, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the idea of an AI "notification mechanism" that could lead to a shared vision of the technology between the largest economies in the world.
But since Sunday's announcement, questions have emerged about what this new mechanism would mean in practice — if it even comes to pass — as China has been silent on embracing the idea.
"Neither side trusts each other, and so they're making these sort of general symbolic promises that look good but have no details behind them," James Lewis of the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday.
He added that any increased communication is a good thing, but every indication is that this will fall short of a "hotline" that serves as a direct connection between the two governments.
Instead, he said, the proposal "sounds pretty informal and I don't think that there's a desire right now to go beyond that."
Yet this effort at increased communication has emerged as the most likely area of agreement on artificial intelligence in the summit, which continues through Friday and will also feature talks on trade, the war in Iran, and many other issues.
Both the US and China have shown little interest in more wide-ranging moves on AI, such as regulating frontier models.
President Trump formally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US on Wednesday evening with an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
The ceremony, according to the White House, featured a 100 foot-long red carpet, the United States Air Force Band, and a flyover from two B1 flyovers, among other touches.
A report in Politico on Tuesday described the notification system as little more than an informal plan to stay in touch, after Bessent described it slightly differently in an appearance on CNBC, calling it a "line so that we have constant communications, especially in the event of some kind of an incident."
Either way, it appeared far short of past direct forms of government-to-government communication, such as the Moscow–Washington hotline, which facilitated communication during the Cold War and was established by a presidential action in 1963.
Bessent suggested that discussion this week would be focused toward further face-to-face talks at the "USA-China AI dialogues" set for November in Shenzhen, in southeastern China.
Other observers echoed the sentiment that this week might not yield a major step forward — but that increased communication could pay dividends down the road.
Chris McGuire of the Council on Foreign Relations described a potential agreement on a communication channel as a "minor" step.
The proposal, he added, is "a credible first step and represents the extent of what is currently possible."
Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution added that "small steps can pave the way for further progress down the road."
As for short-term financial impacts, Jeffries downplayed those effects in a note, telling clients, "even if agreed, the market impact should be limited, since this is disclosure rather than restraint."
The skepticism comes after Bessent said on Sunday that the new form of communication would help relations.
"We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats," Bessent said, while China has offered little of its intentions, such as whether it even wants new communications.
Chinese state media provided a cursory summary of the weekend talks, saying only that Bessent and the Vice Premier He Lifeng held constructive talks on issues "relating to AI" without any further specifics.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

American defense officials are investigating how components from the nation's most advanced stealth aircraft arrived in Hong Kong, after media reports said China obtained F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office acknowledged in a statement that it and the Defense Department are dealing with "a shipment issue" involving parts for the jet.
"We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence," the office stated.
Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles confirmed that the jet components had landed in Hong Kong, though he denied that the missing items were "sensitive equipment." Australia is among several nations whose militaries operate the stealth aircraft.
"Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this," Marles said.
He added: "My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred."
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, as Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. Requests for comment were also submitted to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after a delivery originating in Australia and bound for the United States for repair or disposal months ago was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong. It remains unclear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that the situation prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could gain access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has maintained firm control over Hong Kong since it returned the territory from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas roughly 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been built and 19 countries have placed orders for the aircraft, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China may already have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, regarding the planes. The Defense Science Board, an advisory body to the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is "widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet," according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are continuously updated and improved, counteracting any potential secrets compromised years ago.
Categorized as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings, advanced radar, and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service. Bowman said the plane features advanced sensors to better detect adversaries as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.
